title: Superposition of Waves
short_intro: The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. This fundamental principle explains phenomena such as interference, stationary waves, and beats.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic principle of superposition, graphical addition of waves, constructive and destructive interference, conditions for sustained interference, formation of standing waves in strings and air columns, and beats.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of superposition of two waves with phase difference, intensity distribution in interference, superposition of perpendicular simple harmonic motions (Lissajous figures), and reflection and transmission of waves at boundaries.

prerequisites: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and phase relationships
Wave equation and wave parameters (wavelength, frequency, wave velocity)
Trigonometric identities for sum and difference of angles

concept_notes.heading: Principle of Superposition
bullets: If two or more waves travel simultaneously through a medium, each wave acts independently of the others as if no other waves are present.
The net displacement y(x, t) at any point and at any instant is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements y_1(x, t) and y_2(x, t).
Applicable to linear wave equations where the differential operator governing wave propagation is linear.

concept_notes.heading: Constructive and Destructive Interference
bullets: Constructive interference occurs when waves arrive in phase, resulting in a maximum displacement and maximum intensity.
Destructive interference occurs when waves arrive out of phase (phase difference of odd multiples of π), resulting in minimum displacement and minimum intensity.
The condition for constructive interference is path difference Δx = nλ and phase difference Δφ = 2nπ.

concept_notes.heading: Standing Waves (Stationary Waves)
bullets: Formed by the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions with the same frequency and amplitude.
Nodes are points of zero displacement and maximum pressure variation; antinodes are points of maximum displacement and zero pressure variation.
Energy is not propagated along the medium; it remains confined between nodes.

concept_notes.heading: Beats Phenomenon
bullets: Produced by the superposition of two sound waves of slightly different frequencies traveling in the same direction.
The resultant intensity rises and falls periodically, creating an audible pulsing sound.
The beat frequency is equal to the absolute difference between the two component frequencies: f_b = |f_1 - f_2|.

derivations.title: Superposition of Two Harmonic Waves with Phase Difference
derivations.conditions: Two sinusoidal waves of equal amplitude (A) and frequency (ω) traveling in the same direction with a constant phase difference (φ).
steps: Let the first wave be y_1 = A sin(ωt) and the second wave be y_2 = A sin(ωt + φ).
Using the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement is y = y_1 + y_2 = A [sin(ωt) + sin(ωt + φ)].
Apply trigonometric identity for sum of sines: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A-B)/2).
Substitute the terms: y = 2A cos(φ/2) sin(ωt + φ/2).
Let R = 2A cos(φ/2) be the amplitude of the resultant wave.
derivations.result: y = R sin(ωt + φ/2) where R = 2A cos(φ/2)

derivations.title: Intensity Distribution in Interference
derivations.conditions: Two interfering waves with amplitudes A_1 and A_2 and phase difference φ.
steps: Resultant amplitude squared is R_2 = A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1 A_2 cos(φ) from vector addition.
Since intensity I is proportional to the square of the amplitude (I ∝ A^2), substitute I_1 ∝ A_1^2 and I_2 ∝ A_2^2.
Express resultant intensity as I = I_1 + I_2 + 2√(I_1 I_2) cos(φ).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Graphical Superposition of Pulses
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two triangular wave pulses traveling towards each other on a string, showing overlap and temporary reinforcement/cancellation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At the instant of overlap, the vertical heights add algebraically. After passing each other, both pulses continue unchanged in shape and velocity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in TGT to check conceptual understanding of wave independence after interaction.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Standing Wave Profile
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Envelopes of a string fixed at both ends showing multiple loops with clearly marked nodes (N) and antinodes (A).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates spatial confinement of energy with alternating points of zero and maximum vibration amplitude.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems on harmonics in strings.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Quincke's Tube Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: U-shaped sliding tube apparatus with a sound source and detector demonstrating acoustic interference.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Changing the path length of one tube shifts the sound from loud to soft, proving the wave nature of sound and interference.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions based on path difference calculation to observe intensity minima/maxima.

solved_numericals.question: Two sound waves given by equations y_1 = 0.3 sin(500πt) and y_2 = 0.4 cos(500πt) superimpose. Find the amplitude of the resulting wave.
solution_steps: Rewrite y_2 in sine form: y_2 = 0.4 sin(500πt + π/2).
Identify amplitudes A_1 = 0.3, A_2 = 0.4, and phase difference φ = π/2.
Use resultant amplitude formula: R = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2 \cos(\phi)}.

solved_numericals.question: A tuning fork of unknown frequency produces 4 beats per second with a standard fork of frequency 384 Hz. When a little wax is added to the unknown fork, the beat frequency becomes 6 beats per second. Find the original frequency of the unknown fork.
solution_steps: Let the unknown frequency be f. Given |f - 384| = 4, so f = 388 Hz or 380 Hz.
Adding wax increases the mass, which decreases the frequency of the unknown fork.

If original frequency was 388 Hz, decreasing it would make the new frequency closer to or further from 384 Hz. Test new frequency: if f' < 388, say 386 Hz, beat frequency with 384 Hz is 2 Hz (decreased). But question states beat frequency becomes 6 Hz.
If original frequency was 380 Hz, decreasing it (e.g., to 378 Hz) increases the beat frequency with 384 Hz to |378 - 384| = 6 Hz.
Therefore, the original frequency must be 380 Hz.

solved_numericals.question: The intensity ratio of two coherent waves is 9:1. Find the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in the interference pattern.
solution_steps: Let intensities be I_1 and I_2, such that I_1/I_2 = 9/1.
Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the amplitude ratio A_1/A_2 = \sqrt{9/1} = 3/1.

assumptions_and_limitations: The principle of superposition strictly holds for linear systems where the restoring force is strictly proportional to displacement (Hooke's Law).
Non-linear effects (such as shock waves or finite-amplitude acoustic waves) violate simple linear superposition and lead to harmonic generation and wave steepening.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Waves bounce off each other when they collide during superposition.
common_misconceptions.correct: Waves pass right through each other without altering their individual identities or velocities.
common_misconceptions.why: Interference affects only the displacement at the point of overlap during the encounter, not the permanent state of the individual propagating waves.

common_misconceptions.correct: Energy is conserved; it is redistributed from points of destructive interference (minima) to points of constructive interference (maxima).
common_misconceptions.why: Total integrated energy across the interference pattern remains constant.

quick_revision: Stationary wave nodes are separated by λ/2.
